title: Part 1, Chapter 7
paragraphs: The door opened a crack, as before, and once again two sharp, suspicious eyes peered out at him from the darkness. Then Raskolnikov lost his nerve and nearly made a catastrophic mistake.

Afraid the old woman would be frightened at finding them alone together, and not trusting that the sight of him would calm her suspicions, he grabbed the edge of the door and pulled it toward him to prevent her from slamming it shut. She didn't pull back, but she didn't let go of the handle either, so that he nearly dragged her out onto the landing. Seeing that she was blocking the doorway and wouldn't let him pass, he walked straight toward her. She stumbled backward in alarm, tried to speak, but seemed unable to get the words out. She stared at him with wide eyes.

"Good evening, Alyona Ivanovna," he began, trying to sound casual, but his voice wouldn't cooperate -- it cracked and shook. "I've come... I've brought something... but we should step inside... to the light...."
Without waiting for her, he walked straight into the room. The old woman hurried after him, suddenly finding her tongue.
"Good heavens! What is this? Who is it? What do you want?"
"Alyona Ivanovna, you know me... Raskolnikov... here, I brought the pledge I mentioned the other day...." He held out the package.

The old woman glanced briefly at the pledge, then fixed her eyes on her uninvited visitor. She stared at him -- intently, viciously, suspiciously. A minute passed. He even thought he caught something like a sneer in her eyes, as though she had already guessed everything. He felt himself losing control, felt himself growing terrified -- so terrified that if she kept staring at him like that without saying a word for another half minute, he was sure he would bolt.
"Why are you looking at me as if you don't know me?" he said suddenly, with an edge of hostility. "Take it if you want it. If not, I'll go elsewhere. I'm in a hurry."
He hadn't planned to say this at all -- the words had come out on their own. The old woman recovered herself. Her visitor's firm tone apparently restored her confidence.
"But what's the rush, sir? What is it?" she asked, examining the pledge.
"The silver cigarette case -- the one I mentioned last time, remember."
She held out her hand.
"But how pale you are, really... and your hands are trembling! Have you been swimming or something?"
"Fever," he answered abruptly. "You can't help being pale... when you haven't eaten." He could barely get the words out.
His strength was failing again. But his answer sounded plausible, and the old woman took the pledge.
"What is this?" she asked once more, studying Raskolnikov closely and weighing the package in her hand.
"A thing... cigarette case.... Silver.... Look at it."
"Doesn't look much like silver.... How he's wrapped it up!"

Trying to untie the string, she turned toward the window for better light -- all her windows were shut despite the stifling heat -- and stepped away from him entirely, standing with her back to him for several seconds. He unbuttoned his coat and freed the axe from the loop, but didn't pull it all the way out. He held it in his right hand under the coat. His hands were terrifyingly weak -- he could feel them growing more numb and wooden with every second. He was afraid the axe would slip and clatter to the floor.... A wave of dizziness swept over him.
"What's he gone and wrapped this up for?" the old woman cried in irritation, and turned back toward him.

There was not another instant to lose. He pulled the axe completely free, raised it with both hands, barely conscious of himself, and almost effortlessly, almost mechanically, brought the blunt side down on her head. He seemed not to have used his own strength. But the moment the axe struck, his strength returned.

The old woman was bareheaded as always. Her thin, light hair, streaked with gray and heavily greased, was twisted into a rat-tail braid held in place by a broken horn comb that jutted from the back of her neck. Because she was so short, the blow landed squarely on the crown of her skull. She cried out -- but very faintly -- and instantly crumpled to the floor, raising her hands toward her head. In one hand she still clutched "the pledge." He struck her again, and then again, with the blunt side, on the same spot. Blood poured out as from an overturned glass. The body fell backward. He stepped away, let it fall, and immediately bent over her face. She was dead. Her eyes seemed ready to pop from their sockets. Her forehead and whole face were twisted in a convulsive grimace.

He set the axe on the floor beside the body and immediately felt in her pocket -- trying to avoid the spreading blood -- the same right-hand pocket from which she had taken the key during his last visit. He was in full possession of his faculties, free of confusion or dizziness, though his hands were still trembling. He remembered afterward that he had been remarkably collected and careful, trying the whole time not to get blood on himself.... He pulled out the keys at once -- all of them, as before, on a single steel ring. He ran with them into the bedroom. It was a very small room, with an entire wall covered in icons. Against the far wall stood a large bed, very clean, covered with a silk patchwork quilt. Against a third wall was a chest of drawers. Strangely, the moment he began fitting the keys into the lock, the moment he heard them jingling, a convulsive shudder passed through him. He suddenly felt tempted to abandon everything and leave. But that lasted only an instant -- it was too late to go back. He actually smiled at himself. Then another terrifying thought struck him. He suddenly imagined that the old woman might still be alive and could regain consciousness. Leaving the keys in the chest, he rushed back to the body, snatched up the axe, and raised it over the old woman again -- but didn't bring it down. There was no doubt she was dead. Bending down for a closer look, he could clearly see that the skull was smashed, even caved in on one side. He started to touch it with his finger but pulled his hand back -- the evidence was clear enough without that. Meanwhile, a large pool of blood had formed. He suddenly noticed a cord around her neck. He tugged at it, but the cord was strong and wouldn't snap, and besides, it was soaked in blood. He tried to pull it out from the front of her dress, but something caught and held it. In his impatience he raised the axe to cut the cord from above, against the body, but didn't dare. With difficulty, getting blood on his hands and the axe, he managed after two minutes of frantic effort to cut the string without touching the body with the blade. He was right -- it was a purse. On the cord hung two crosses, one of cypress wood and one of copper, and a small silver filigree icon, along with a little, greasy chamois leather purse with a steel clasp and ring. The purse was crammed full. Raskolnikov shoved it in his pocket without looking at it, dropped the crosses onto the old woman's body, and rushed back into the bedroom, this time carrying the axe.

He was in a frantic rush. He grabbed the keys and started trying them again, but without success. They wouldn't fit. It wasn't so much that his hands were shaking -- he kept making mistakes. He could see, for instance, that a key wasn't the right one and wouldn't fit, yet he kept trying to force it in. Suddenly he remembered something: the large key with the deep notches, which hung with the smaller ones, couldn't possibly belong to the chest of drawers -- this had occurred to him during his last visit too -- it must be for some kind of strongbox, and that was probably where everything was hidden. He abandoned the chest of drawers and immediately felt under the bed, knowing that old women usually keep boxes under their beds. And there it was: a good-sized box under the bed, at least a yard long, with an arched lid covered in red leather and studded with steel nails. The notched key fit immediately and unlocked it. On top, under a white sheet, lay a red brocade coat lined with hare fur; under that a silk dress, then a shawl -- and below that, nothing but clothes, it seemed. The first thing he did was wipe his bloody hands on the red brocade. "It's red, and blood will be less noticeable on red," the thought passed through his mind. Then he caught himself. "My God, am I losing my mind?" he thought in terror.

But the moment he touched the clothes, a gold watch slid out from under the fur coat. He hurried to turn everything over. Sure enough, scattered among the clothing were various gold items -- probably all unredeemed or not-yet-redeemed pledges -- bracelets, chains, earrings, pins, and the like. Some were in cases, others simply wrapped in newspaper, neatly and precisely folded and tied with string. Without pausing to examine or open the packages and cases, he began stuffing them into the pockets of his trousers and overcoat. But he didn't have time to take many....

Suddenly he heard footsteps in the room where the old woman lay. He froze, motionless as death. But all was quiet -- he must have imagined it. Then he clearly heard a faint cry, as if someone had let out a soft, broken moan. Then silence again for a minute or two. He crouched by the box, holding his breath. Then he leapt to his feet, grabbed the axe, and ran out of the bedroom.

In the middle of the room stood Lizaveta, holding a large bundle. She was staring in stupefaction at her murdered sister, white as a sheet, apparently without the strength to scream. Seeing him burst from the bedroom, she began trembling all over, faintly, like a leaf. A shudder ran across her face. She raised one hand, opened her mouth, but still made no sound. She began backing slowly away from him toward the corner, staring at him steadily, fixedly, but still not making a sound -- as though she couldn't draw enough breath to scream. He rushed at her with the axe. Her mouth twitched pitifully, the way babies' mouths do when they start to get frightened, staring wide-eyed at whatever scares them, on the verge of crying out. This wretched Lizaveta was so simple and so thoroughly crushed and terrified that she didn't even raise a hand to shield her face -- the most necessary, most natural gesture in the world, with the axe poised above her. She only lifted her empty left hand, slowly, not to her face but holding it out in front of her as if pushing him away. The blade of the axe came down directly on her skull and split the entire top of her head in a single blow. She collapsed heavily, instantly. Raskolnikov completely lost his head. He snatched up her bundle, dropped it again, and ran for the door.

Terror seized him more and more powerfully, especially after this second, utterly unexpected murder. He wanted to flee the place as fast as he could. If in that moment he had been capable of clearer thought -- of grasping the full difficulty of his position, its hopelessness, its horror, its absurdity -- of understanding how many obstacles and perhaps how many more crimes he still had to overcome to escape and make it home -- he might well have abandoned everything and gone to turn himself in. And not from fear, but from pure horror and revulsion at what he had done. Revulsion above all surged inside him, growing stronger every minute. Nothing in the world would have made him go back to the strongbox or even into that room.

But a kind of blankness, a dreamlike stupor, was gradually taking hold of him. At moments he forgot himself -- or rather, forgot what was important and latched onto trivialities. Glancing into the kitchen, however, and seeing a bucket half-full of water on a bench, he thought to wash his hands and the axe. His hands were sticky with blood. He dropped the axe blade-first into the water, grabbed a piece of soap from a cracked saucer on the windowsill, and began washing his hands in the bucket. When they were clean, he pulled out the axe, washed the blade, and spent a long time -- about three minutes -- scrubbing the wooden handle where there were bloodstains, rubbing them with soap. Then he wiped everything with a piece of linen hanging on a line in the kitchen, and stood for a long while examining the axe carefully by the window. No trace remained -- only the wood was still damp. He carefully hung the axe back in the loop under his coat. Then, as well as he could in the dim kitchen light, he checked his overcoat, trousers, and boots. At first glance there seemed to be nothing -- only some spots on the boots. He wet the rag and rubbed them. But he knew he wasn't being thorough, that there might be something clearly visible that he was missing. He stood in the middle of the room, lost in thought. Dark, agonizing ideas crowded his mind -- the idea that he was going mad, that at this moment he was incapable of reasoning, of protecting himself, that perhaps he should be doing something entirely different from what he was doing. "My God!" he whispered. "I have to get out of here, get out!" He rushed to the entryway. But there a shock of terror awaited him unlike anything he had ever experienced.

He stood and stared, unable to believe his eyes: the front door -- the outer door to the staircase, where he had stood ringing the bell not long ago -- was open. Standing wide open, at least six inches ajar. No lock, no bolt, the entire time! The old woman hadn't shut it after letting him in -- perhaps as a precaution against being left alone with him. But my God! He had seen Lizaveta come in afterward! And how -- how had he not realized that she must have entered somehow? She couldn't have come through the wall!
He rushed to the door and slid the bolt home.
"No, wrong again! I have to get out, get out...."
He unfastened the bolt, opened the door, and listened on the staircase.

He listened for a long time. Somewhere far below -- maybe at the gate -- two voices were shouting loudly and shrilly, quarreling and cursing. "What's that about?" He waited patiently. At last everything went quiet, as if suddenly cut off. They had gone their separate ways. He was about to step out when suddenly, on the floor below, a door banged open and someone started down the stairs, humming a tune. "Why do they all make so much noise?" flashed through his mind. He closed the door again and waited. Finally everything was still -- not a soul. He had just taken a step toward the staircase when he heard more footsteps.

The steps sounded very far away, at the very bottom of the stairs, but he remembered clearly and distinctly that from the first sound, he began to suspect for some reason that this person was coming _here_ -- to the fourth floor, to the old woman's apartment. Why? Was there something distinctive, something meaningful about the footsteps? They were heavy, steady, unhurried. Now the person had passed the first floor. Now climbing higher -- closer and clearer. He could hear the heavy breathing. Now the third floor.... Coming here! And suddenly it felt as though he had been turned to stone -- like in a dream where you're being chased, nearly caught, about to be killed, and you're rooted to the spot, unable to even move your arms.

At last, when the unknown person was climbing to the fourth floor, Raskolnikov suddenly jerked to life. He managed to slip neatly and quickly back into the apartment and close the door behind him. Then he took the hook and noiselessly fitted it into the catch. Instinct guided him. When it was done, he crouched by the door, holding his breath. The unknown visitor was now at the door too. They stood on opposite sides, just as Raskolnikov had stood with the old woman moments before -- separated by the door, listening.
The visitor drew several heavy breaths. "Must be a big, heavy man," Raskolnikov thought, gripping the axe. It all felt like a dream. The visitor took hold of the bell and rang it loudly.

The instant the tin bell tinkled, Raskolnikov thought he heard something moving in the apartment. For several seconds he listened in dead earnest. The stranger rang again, waited, then suddenly and violently yanked at the door handle. Raskolnikov watched the hook bouncing in its catch with horror, expecting at every moment that it would be torn free. It certainly seemed possible, given how violently the man was shaking it. He was tempted to hold the catch in place, but the man might feel the resistance. Dizziness swept over him. "I'm going to collapse!" flashed through his mind. But the stranger began to speak, and he recovered instantly.

"What the hell? Are they asleep or dead in there? Damn them!" the man bellowed in a thick voice. "Hey, Alyona Ivanovna, you old witch! Lizaveta Ivanovna, you beauty! Open the door! Damn them! Are they asleep or what?"
Enraged, he yanked the bell a dozen more times with all his strength. He was clearly a man of some authority and a close acquaintance.
At that moment quick, light footsteps were heard not far off, on the stairs. Someone else was approaching. Raskolnikov hadn't noticed at first.
"Nobody home? Really?" the newcomer called out in a cheerful, ringing voice, addressing the first visitor, who was still pulling at the bell. "Evening, Koch."
"Must be quite young, judging by the voice," Raskolnikov thought.
"Who the hell knows? I've nearly broken the lock," Koch answered. "But how do you know me?"
"Come on! The day before yesterday I beat you three games straight at billiards, at Gambrinus's."
"Oh!"
"So they're not home? That's weird. Awfully stupid, though. Where would the old woman go? I came here on business."
"I have business with her too."
"Well, what can we do? Go back, I guess. Damn! And I was hoping to get some money!" the young man exclaimed.

"We'll have to give up, of course, but why did she set this time herself? The old witch picked the time! It's out of my way. And where on earth could she have gone? She sits in this apartment year in, year out, the old hag -- her legs are bad -- and all of a sudden she's out for a walk!"
"Should we ask the porter?"
"About what?"
"Where she went and when she'll be back."
"Hmm.... Damn it all.... We could ask.... But she never goes anywhere."
He tugged at the door handle once more.
"Damn it all! Nothing to be done. Let's go."
"Wait!" the young man said suddenly. "Look -- see how the door moves when you pull it?"
"So?"
"That means it's not locked with a key -- it's latched with the hook! Can you hear the hook rattling?"
"So?"

"Don't you see? That proves someone is home. If they were all out, they would have locked the door from the outside with the key, not hooked it from the inside. Listen to the hook rattling! To fasten the hook, someone has to be inside. So they're sitting in there and not opening the door!"
"Right! You're right!" Koch cried, astonished. "What are they doing in there?" He began shaking the door furiously.
"Wait!" the young man said again. "Stop pulling. Something's wrong here.... You've been ringing and banging and they still won't open! Either they've both fainted or..."
"What?"
"Here's what we do. Let's go get the porter and have him wake them up."
"All right."
They started downstairs.
"Wait -- you stay here while I run down for the porter."
"Why?"
"Just trust me."
"All right."
"I'm studying law, you see! It's obvious, ob-vi-ous that something is wrong here!" the young man shouted excitedly, and ran downstairs.

Koch stayed behind. He softly touched the bell, which gave a single tinkle. Then gently, as though thinking it over and examining the situation, he began working the door handle -- pulling it and releasing it -- to confirm once more that the door was only latched with a hook. Then, puffing and panting, he bent down and tried to peer through the keyhole. But the key was in the lock on the inside, so nothing was visible.

Raskolnikov stood gripping the axe. He was in something like delirium. He was even prepared to fight them when they came in. While they were knocking and talking, the idea of ending it all flashed through his mind several times -- to fling open the door and shout at them. At moments he wanted to curse them, taunt them, while they still couldn't get in. "Just hurry up!" was the thought that kept racing through his head.
"But what the devil is he doing?..." Time passed. One minute, another -- nobody came. Koch grew restless.
"What the hell!" he suddenly burst out, and abandoning his post in a fit of impatience, he too clattered downstairs, his heavy boots thumping on the steps. The footsteps faded.
"My God! What do I do?"
Raskolnikov unhooked the latch, opened the door -- silence. Without thinking, without any thought at all, he stepped out, pulled the door shut as carefully as he could, and went downstairs.
He had gone down three flights when he suddenly heard a loud commotion below. Where could he go? There was nowhere to hide. He was about to turn back to the apartment.
"Hey! Stop him! Catch him!"
Someone burst out of an apartment below, shouting, and practically fell rather than ran down the stairs, bellowing at the top of his lungs:
"Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Damn him!"

The shout ended in a shriek. The last sounds came from the courtyard. Then silence. But at the same moment several men began noisily climbing the stairs, talking loudly and rapidly. There were three or four of them. He recognized the young man's ringing voice. "Them!"

Filled with despair, he walked straight toward them, thinking: "Whatever happens, happens!" If they stopped him, it was all over. If they let him pass, it was all over too -- they would remember him. They were getting closer. Only one flight separated them. And then -- salvation! A few steps away on the right, an empty apartment stood with its door wide open -- the second-floor apartment where the painters had been working and which, as if arranged for his benefit, they had just left. It must have been them running down the stairs and shouting. The floor had just been painted. In the middle of the room stood a bucket and a cracked pot with paint and brushes. In an instant he had slipped through the open door and hidden behind the wall -- just in time. They had already reached the landing. Then they turned and continued upstairs to the fourth floor, talking loudly. He waited, tiptoed out, and ran down the stairs.
No one was on the staircase. No one was at the gate. He passed quickly through the gateway and turned left into the street.

He knew -- he knew with perfect certainty -- that at this moment they were in the apartment, that they were astonished to find the door unlatched when it had just been hooked, that by now they were looking at the bodies, and that within another minute they would realize the murderer had just been there, had hidden somewhere, slipped past them, and escaped. They would almost certainly guess he had been in the empty apartment while they were going upstairs. And yet he didn't dare walk any faster, though the next turning was still nearly a hundred yards away. "Should I duck into some gateway and wait on an unfamiliar street? No, hopeless! Should I throw away the axe? Take a cab? Hopeless, hopeless!"

At last he reached the corner. He turned down it more dead than alive. Here he was halfway to safety, and he knew it: it was less risky because there was a dense crowd, and he disappeared into it like a grain of sand. But everything he had been through had drained him so completely that he could barely move. Sweat ran down him in drops; his neck was soaked. "That fellow's had quite a workout!" someone called out as he emerged at the canal embankment.

His awareness was fading now, and the farther he went, the worse it got. He did remember, however, that coming out onto the canal bank, he was alarmed at how few people there were -- making him more conspicuous -- and he thought about turning back. Though he was nearly collapsing from exhaustion, he took a long detour to reach home from a completely different direction.

He was barely conscious when he passed through the gateway of his building! He was already on the staircase before he remembered the axe. And yet he faced a very serious problem: returning it while attracting as little attention as possible. He was, of course, incapable of considering that it might be far better not to return the axe at all, but simply to drop it later in someone's yard. But everything worked out fortunately. The porter's door was closed but not locked, which probably meant the porter was home. But he had so completely lost the ability to think that he walked straight to the door and opened it. If the porter had asked, "What do you want?" he might simply have handed him the axe. But once again the porter wasn't there. He managed to put the axe back under the bench, covering it with the block of wood as before. He didn't meet a soul after that, all the way to his room. The landlady's door was shut. When he reached his room, he threw himself on the sofa just as he was. He didn't sleep, but sank into a blank oblivion. If anyone had entered his room then, he would have leapt up screaming. Fragments and scraps of thoughts swarmed in his brain, but he couldn't hold onto any of them, couldn't settle on a single one, no matter how hard he tried....
